bio.en: A special compilation episode in which Lenny revisits the most insightful stories of failure pulled from past conversations, arguing that you can often learn more from failure than from studying successful companies.
bio.zh: 这是一期特别的合集节目：Lenny 从过往对话中挑出最具启发性的“失败”故事重新编排，主张研究失败往往比研究成功公司更能学到东西。

summary.en: Instead of a standard interview, this episode curates the best failure stories from across the podcast's back catalog into one focused listen. Lenny makes the case that studying how things break—rather than only how the best companies operate—yields some of the most valuable lessons for builders. It's an experiment in thematic compilation, and Lenny invites listener feedback to decide whether to keep doing more like it.

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: I'm happy to talk about it because frankly, it was the biggest learning experience of my leadership career, or at least that happened in one moment, and it happened in my early days at Airbnb. So I was hired to take on the experience design organization, that's basically the product design team, which was 10 people at the time. (00:04:02): And so they had been reporting directly to one of the founders and they were going to start reporting to me. And during my interview process, I learned a lot about what was working and what wasn't working and some of the trials and tribulations with the design organization and its collaboration with others. So it seemed like there was room for improvement in how engineering and product management and design all work together. And there was also really low engagement scores in the design team. (00:04:29): And so I came in ready to go and excited to try to help make some change based on all the things that I had learned from various leaders and people across the company. And I came in swinging ready to go, and then about a month into my time there, I got a meeting on my calendar. Thursday 8:30 AM, was an hour and a half with half of the design team, so that was five people, and our HR partner.
turns.zh: 很乐意聊聊这段经历，因为说实话，这是我领导生涯中最深刻的学习经历——至少在Airbnb的早期阶段，那一刻的顿悟意义非凡。当时我受命接管体验设计团队（即产品设计部门），该团队当时由10人组成。（00:04:02）之前他们一直直接向公司创始人汇报工作，而现在要改为向我汇报。在面试过程中，我深入了解了设计团队的运作现状、存在的痛点，以及与其他部门协作中的挑战。很明显，工程、产品管理和设计部门之间的协作机制亟待优化，同时设计团队的敬业度也处于低谷。（00:04:29）带着满腔热情，我接手后决心基于从各级领导和公司内外人士那里汲取的经验，推动变革。然而上任仅一个月后，日程表上就安排了一场会议：周四上午8:30，与设计团队半数成员（共5人）及人力资源伙伴进行长达一个半小时的沟通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, no. That's never a good sign.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。这可不是个好兆头。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Usually it's [inaudible 00:05:01]. Yeah. And I remember this so vividly. I remember walking into the office and all the rooms in Airbnb's office are very unique spaces that look like Airbnbs, but of course this was the one room with all white walls and just a gray flat rectangle table. And I walked into the room and there were five of them seated around the table and they had a pack of papers in front of them, and they went on taking turns quietly reading from the papers all the things that they saw that I was doing wrong and all the things that they didn't like about me. And it was a really hard moment there. I went through all the usual stages of grief when one hears feedback, which is just immediate want to respond to be like, "Oh, well there was a good reason for that." And, "That's not how it actually was," and, "This is why I did that." (00:05:59): But luckily I had, thank goodness, I had the sense to just listen and not respond in that way. Clearly, what they were telling me is that that was one of the things that was missing. And so I heard them out and took it all in. And regardless of each individual thing, what was very clear was that the missing piece, the theme that was across all of that is that I hadn't earned their trust. So whether how right or how wrong what I was doing was is the key piece is that I wasn't bringing the team along with me. They had no idea that they could trust in what I was trying to build and what I was trying to shape and that I cared about them and that I had their best interest and shared goals at heart. And that was absolutely my fault. (00:06:45): And in retrospect, as hard as that was, I'm very grateful and very amazed that they could come together and share that with me. It can be hard to bring feedback forward like that. (00:06:57): And so it was an extremely valuable learning experience and I took from that to then immediately shift how I was operating. And really a key part in building trust was to listen, to hear out what the individuals on the team were setting out to do, what they cared about, what motivated them. And so I started to make pretty fast change and still moving in the direction that was necessary for the org to make the really large impact in how we were operating, but bringing folks along with me. You can inflict change on people, but if you want to do it with them, really trust is the key element there. (00:07:37): And then a couple of months later, we had the best engagement scores in the company. So it actually, it did objectively improve the situation and since then taken that on into next steps in other companies that I've joined and just think about instead of coming in swinging, come in listening, so that you can really set out to make change that actually has true positive impact on the folks around you and you bring along with you.
turns.zh: 通常情况下（00:05:01），嗯。我对这件事记忆犹新。我记得走进Airbnb办公室时，那里的每个房间都别具特色，布置得像民宿一样。但当然，那间办公室唯一一间全白墙壁、只有灰色长方形桌子的房间除外。我走进房间时，看到五个人围坐在桌旁，面前放着一叠文件。他们轮流安静地朗读着我做错的所有事情，以及他们不喜欢我的地方。那真是一个艰难的时刻。当听到反馈时，我会经历所有常见的悲伤阶段——比如急于反驳说“哦，那肯定有合理的理由”，或者说“事实并非如此”，或者“这就是我当时的初衷”。（00:05:59）但幸运的是，我庆幸自己当时保持了清醒的头脑，选择倾听而非反驳。他们显然在告诉我，这是我所欠缺的部分之一。因此，我耐心听完他们的意见，仔细领会其中的要点。抛开具体细节不谈，最关键的是我没有赢得他们的信任。无论我的做法是对是错，核心问题在于我没有让团队与我同行。他们完全不了解我试图打造的产品，他们关心的是我是否在乎他们，是否把他们的最大利益和共同目标放在心上。这完全是我的过错。（00:06:45）回想起来，尽管那段经历很痛苦，但我非常感激他们能勇敢地站出来与我分享反馈。坦诚地提出意见并非易事。（00:06:57）这是一次极其宝贵的学习经历，我立刻改变了自己的工作方式。建立信任的关键在于倾听，了解团队成员的目标、关切和动力。因此，我迅速做出调整，继续朝着必要的方向前进，为组织带来重大影响，同时让团队成员全心投入。（00:07:37）几个月后，我们创下了公司最佳员工敬业度评分记录。这确实客观地改善了局面。此后，我加入的其他公司也沿用了这一方法——不再强制推行变革，而是以信任为核心，倾听各方意见，共同推动变革，最终为身边的人创造积极影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next up, Paul Adams, chief product Officer at Intercom, sharing the nightmare experience of freezing on stage in front of thousands of people, having to walk off stage, and then people hearing him curse because the mic was still on, and then how he recovered. Plus a few stories of building some of Google's most infamous product failures.
turns.zh: 接下来是Intercom的首席产品官保罗·亚当斯（Paul Adams），他将分享在数千人面前登台却卡壳、不得不退场，以及麦克风未关闭导致观众听到他爆粗口的噩梦经历。还有他如何从中恢复的故事，以及他在谷歌打造一些最臭名昭著的产品失败案例的经历。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Some things have happened in work, are very memorable at the time and they don't really scar you. This goes in the book that have scarred for life. Yeah, let's go long story short, I was at Facebook just over a decade ago, loved it at the time. I think it was a great place to be at the time. And basically San Francisco, I did a lot of talks for Facebook internally and externally. Facebook had a keynote slot, always have a keynote slot at Cannes, the world's biggest advertising festival. And the year prior, Zuck had been interviewed. He was the speaker, he'd been interviewed, gotten a hard time on privacy. It didn't go well, as well as they'd hoped. (00:09:00): So the next year they asked me to do it, maybe it was the Irish accent that made the offer come my way. And yeah, I got out into front the stage of the world's biggest advertising stage, and I'd say I was like three or four minutes into the talk, a talk I'd given, a very similar talk that I'd given lots of times. (00:09:19): And I just froze. I couldn't remember what I was supposed to say. It was the first ever time in my life I'd rehearsed a talk word for word. Usually, I have talking points and I'd ad lib and things get mixed around and it's kind of informal. This was media trained, do not say the wrong thing kind of talk. And I just could not remember what to say. I had some version of a panic attack, walked off stage, I was still mic'd up, cursed. I was laughing. I was like, "Geez, are they laughing at me. Oh my God, this is..." But I can manage to turn it around, I walked back out, I'd kind of been disarmed internally in my head, and the rest of it went well. And I was famous that night out in Cannes afterwards on whatever the seafront, it's just like rosé everywhere. I was famous and infamous for my performance.
turns.zh:
工作中确实会遇到一些事，当时觉得印象深刻，但并不会留下永久的创伤。这类经历应该写进那些让你刻骨铭心的书里了。是啊，说长不说短，大约十多年前我在Facebook工作，当时很喜欢那儿，觉得那是个很棒的工作环境。尤其是在旧金山，我经常为Facebook内部和外部做演讲。Facebook在戛纳这个全球最大的广告节上一直有主场发言的机会。前一年扎克伯格接受采访时，他作为主讲嘉宾被问及隐私问题，但表现不佳，远未达到预期效果。

（00:09:00）次年他们邀请我上台，或许是因为我的爱尔兰口音而青睐于我。结果在全球最大的广告舞台上，我刚讲了三四分钟，内容和之前多次演讲的模板几乎一模一样。

（00:09:19）突然大脑一片空白，完全记不清该说什么。这是我人生中第一次逐字排练演讲稿。通常我只是准备提纲，随口发挥，内容会混乱又不拘形式。但这次是经过媒体训练的演讲，必须字字正确。我完全记不住台词，经历了轻微的恐慌发作，走下舞台时话筒还戴着，还爆了粗口。当时我在笑，心想：“天啊，他们是在嘲笑我吗？哦，天哪，这真是……”但最终我调整过来，重新走上舞台，虽然内心早已崩溃，但剩下的演讲还算顺利。那晚我在戛纳海边被封神了，到处都是玫瑰酒，我既出名又出丑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you lived the worst nightmare that everybody has when they're thinking about giving a talk. And I think what's interesting is you survived, and I think that's a really interesting lesson is you could freeze in front of thousands of people, walk off stage, and then it works out okay.
turns.zh: 我觉得你经历了每个人演讲时最可怕的噩梦。最有趣的是你挺过来了，从中吸取的教训是，即便在数千人面前卡壳、走下舞台，事情最终也能圆满解决。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: And it all happened organically, I guess, or very naturally. But yeah, ever since then, every time I walk out onto a conference talk stage, still today, I ask myself, I have this tiny doubt in the back of my head. It's never happened since. But yeah, I think you have to go with it with these things. When life kind of throws you these whatever curve balls you have got to kind of adapt, and it's not that big a deal. None of these things are that big a deal. At the end of the day you kind of move on, live and learn. Yeah, but I still hope it doesn't happen again.
turns.zh: 这一切似乎都是自然而然发生的。但从那以后每次登上会议舞台，我都会在内心深处产生一丝疑虑，至今再没出现过那样的情况。不过遇到生活抛来的曲线球时，就随机应变吧，没什么大不了的。最终你总能继续前行，吸取教训。是啊，但我还是希望这种情况别再发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also hate public speaking and I always fear this is exactly what's going to happen to me. And so I think this is nice to hear that even when the worst possible thing basically happens, things can survive.
turns.zh: 我也讨厌公开演讲，总担心自己会遇到同样的情况。听你说即便最糟糕的情况也能挺过去，真是振奋人心。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: You can turn it around. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你总能扭转局面。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A second area I wanted to hear from is your time at Google and there's a couple products you worked on at Google. Both of them were not what you'd call big successes, and then there's kind of a transition to Facebook, which was also kind messy. Can you just share a couple stories from that time?
turns.zh: 接下来我想听听你在谷歌的经历，你参与的两个产品都算不上成功案例，然后过渡到Facebook的混乱时期。能分享一下那段时期的故事吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. Similar to the walking off stage thing, you live and learn, and I was at Google for four years. I was at Facebook for two and a half years or so. At Google I worked on a lot of failed social projects like you mentioned, Google Buzz, Google, and later Google+. I think a lot of the motivation for those projects came from a place of fear. It didn't come from a place of let's make a great product for people,.let's really understand the things people struggle with when communicating with family and friends. That's really, really try and create something wonderful. It came from a place of fear. (00:12:10): And so during those times I learned I think how not to lead in places. And by the way, I should say at the time in Google, there was other things happening that were amazing, like Google building Google Maps. Incredible product, one of my favorite products. I think one of the best products ever made. They were building Android. I was in the mobile team, in the mobile apps team at the time that Android came out. So incredibly good product. So I just happened to be in the social side, which wasn't as good. (00:12:37): And yeah, Google Buzz was kind of a privacy disaster, and Google+ similar. And so kind of halfway through I kind of published research about groups, and I've done a ton of research. An interesting kind of side note there is at the time I asked, I was working in the research, in the US team as a researcher, I was being asked to do a lot of tactical research, like usability study type stuff, like can people use these products? And I ended up doing a lot of formative research as well in the same session. So I'd kind of say to the team like, "Hey, I'll do the research, I'll answer your questions, but also I'm going to do this other thing, and I'm going to take 20 minutes doing that." (00:13:16): And so what we used to do is, what I used to do with people was map out their social network, all the people in it, their family, their friends, how they communicate. We'd map on all the channels, we'd talk about what worked well, what didn't. And we did this with dozens and dozens of people over the course of maybe 18 months. And the same pattern emerged every single time, which was people need way better ways to communicate with small groups of family and friends. And I kind of look back now and go like WhatsApp, or it maybe iMessage if everyone's on Apple, but really obvious in hindsight, but at the time, not obvious. And so we kind of tried to build a product around that called Google+, but again, it was kind of came from the wrong place. And so halfway through the research that I've done, all this research had been made public through a conference talk and Zuck and Facebook noticed, got in touch, one thing led to another and I left and joined Facebook, which was an amazing thing for me, personally. (00:14:13): Facebook was amazing, an amazing place at the time and exciting. And they were trying to do things for the other reasons, the kind of good reasons, like, "Hey, let's build an amazing product for people."
turns.zh: 是的。就像退场那件事一样，人总是要吸取教训的。我在谷歌工作了四年，在Facebook待了两年半左右。在谷歌期间，我参与了很多失败的社交项目，比如你提到的Google Buzz、Google+。这些项目的动机很多时候源于恐惧心理，而不是为了给用户创造出色的产品，或者真正理解人们在与家人朋友交流时面临的难题，努力打造出色的产品。而是出于恐惧。（00:12:10）所以在那段时期，我学会了如何避免在某些方面领导不力。顺便说一句，当时谷歌还有其他令人惊叹的项目，比如开发Google Maps。这是令人惊叹的产品，也是我最喜欢的产品之一。我认为它是史上最出色的产品之一。他们还在开发安卓系统。我当时在移动团队，安卓刚推出时我在移动应用团队工作。这些产品都非常棒。但我恰好在社交领域工作，而那里的表现并不理想。（00:12:37）是的，Google Buzz堪称隐私灾难，Google+也差不多。在项目进行到一半时，我开始研究社交群组，进行了一系列研究。一个有趣的细节是，当时我在美国团队做研究时，被要求做很多战术性研究，比如可用性测试之类的，比如用户是否能使用这些产品。但在同一次会议中，我还做了大量形成性研究。所以我会对团队说：“嘿，我会做研究，回答你们的问题，但我也会做其他事情，每次20分钟。”（00:13:16）我们过去常做的，或者说我过去常做的，是绘制他们的社交网络图，里面所有的人，他们的家人、朋友，以及他们的沟通方式。我们会绘制所有沟通渠道图，讨论哪些有效，哪些无效。我们在18个月的时间里对数十人进行了这样的研究，每次得到的结论都是：人们需要更好的方式与家人朋友的小群组进行沟通。现在回头看，比如WhatsApp，或者如果大家都用苹果设备，可能用iMessage，但事后看来显而易见，但当时并不明显。所以我们试图围绕这个需求打造产品Google+，但同样，出发点错了。研究进行到一半时，我做的所有研究成果通过会议报告公之于众，扎克伯格和Facebook注意到了这些成果，一来二去，我就离开谷歌加入了Facebook，这对我个人来说是个很棒的选择。（00:14:13）Facebook当时是个令人惊叹的地方，令人兴奋不已。他们出于正确的动机做事，比如“嘿，让我们为用户打造出色的产品”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this was during Google+ being built? You basically shifted.
turns.zh: 这是在Google+开发期间吗？你基本上是跳槽了。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, midway, I'm stressed to even telling you about it. The project hadn't been launched. It was still under wraps. It was highly confidential. Google had done a lot of things at the time that were the first for them. I don't know if they've done them since, but things like everyone worked in Google+ was sent to a different building. That building had a different key card. If you didn't work on Google+, you could not get in. All sorts of counter-cultural things at the time. And as a result, there was a lot of antagonism internally for Google+. And so when I left in the middle of the project, leaving with all of the plans in my head to the enemy, some people saw me as a traitor, understandably. Other people thought I was enlightened. It depends on who you talked to, but it was the right thing for me to do. But at the time it was a hard thing to do.
turns.zh: 是啊，中途回想起来，我甚至都不敢跟你提这件事。那个项目当时还没正式启动，还处于保密阶段，高度机密。谷歌当时做了很多开创性的尝试，不知道他们现在是否还在做。比如所有参与Google+项目的员工都被安排到另一栋楼办公，那栋楼有单独的门禁卡，如果你不参与Google+项目，就进不去。当时有各种违背常规的做法。因此，谷歌内部对Google+项目充满了抵触情绪。所以当我在项目中途离开时，带着满脑子的计划投奔竞争对手，一些人觉得我背叛了公司，这可以理解。另一些人则认为我很有远见。不同人有不同看法，但对我来说，这确实是正确的选择。不过当时这确实是个艰难的决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know there's also a lot of scrutiny in what you took with you and the process.
turns.zh: 我知道人们对你的离职动机和项目资料的保管问题也存在诸多质疑。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: When I left, Google kind of assumed that I was one of the spies. I was quarantined when I told them I was leaving. They forensically analyzed my laptop, all sorts of stuff like that. So it was pretty intense. Looking back, I can understand why that happened, but the root cause for me is that the project has been run from a place of fear, competitive fear, which I don't think leads to good things.
turns.zh: 离开谷歌时，他们认定我是内部间谍。告知离职时，他们对我实施了隔离审查，仔细检查了我的笔记本电脑等物品。整个过程相当严苛。回想起来，我能理解他们的担忧，但根本原因在于整个项目从一开始就笼罩在恐惧和竞争的阴影下，我认为这种心态注定难有好结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one of the themes through the stories you just shared is, let's say failure is... I don't want to make it that harsh, but just things not working out. And I'm curious as a product leader, how important you think that is for people to go through if you think that's something that is almost a good thing. And I guess just is there anything there that you find helpful as a coach, as a mentor, as someone, to people that are trying to become basically you?
turns.zh: 从你刚才分享的故事中可以看出，一种主题就是——比如说项目失败，或者说事情没有如愿以偿。我很好奇，作为产品负责人，您认为这种经历对人们来说有多重要？您是否认为这几乎是一种积极的成长体验？作为教练或导师，您能给那些想成为您这样的人一些有益的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: It very, very... It still is. It still is. I've personally failed so many times. There are two stories and the Google one is long deep tentacles. There are two stories. I've failed a ton of times like at Intercom. I remember when I was at Facebook, I was very happy and I knew I wanted to [inaudible 00:16:39] the co-founders of Intercom and they're trying to persuade me to join Intercom. It was like 10 person company at the time. But Owen said something to me at that time, which has stuck with me ever since. He said, "At Facebook you can design the product, but at Intercom you can design the company." And that was extremely appealing to me, a great pitch. He's like, "Just design the company with us that you want to work in." (00:17:03): And so part of that was a company that embraces failure that says it's okay to try things. I'm a big believer in big bets, higher risk, higher reward. I don't get as excited about incremental things. Now I haven't said that, there's of course a place for that too, especially as companies get bigger. But I get excited about big bets and if you make big bets, you're going to get a lot of it wrong. So a lot of the principles that we built here at Intercom, on building software, we have a principle called ship to learn, and we've actually changed it since, still on the wall here. Ship fast, ship early, ship often is what it says now. Used to say ship to learn. Ship fast, ship early, ship often. It's like in that idea is the idea of failure. It's not going to go right, and it's going to go wrong more often than not. But if you ship early and fast and learn fast, you can change fast, and you can improve fast. And that's the kind of culture that we as much as possible try to embrace and teach people. But it's much easier said than done.
turns.zh: 太、太……现在依然如此。我个人失败过很多次。说到这儿，有两个故事，谷歌那次简直是一团乱麻。还有两个故事。我在Intercom的失败经历堪称惨痛。记得在Facebook工作时，我曾深感满足，深知自己想加入Intercom的联合创始人团队——当时那只不过是一家10人的小公司。但欧文当时对我说的一句话让我至今难忘。他说：“在Facebook你可以设计产品，但在Intercom你能设计公司。”这句话对我极具吸引力，是个绝佳的推销说辞。他说：“就和我们一起设计你想工作的公司吧。”（00:17:03）这背后隐藏着一个理念：公司要包容失败，允许尝试新事物。我坚信大胆押注、高风险高回报的理念。面对渐进式改进，我实在提不起兴趣。当然，公司规模越大，这种渐进式改进就越有其存在的价值。但我热衷于大胆尝试，既然要冒险，就难免会出错。我们在Intercom建立的软件开发理念叫“快速上线以学习”，不过后来我们调整了表述，现在墙上写着“快速上线、快速迭代、快速学习”。其核心理念就是允许失败。大多数尝试都会出错，但早期快速上线、快速迭代、快速学习就能快速改进。这正是我们努力践行并传授给员工的文化。但说起来容易做起来难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Especially when you're in the moment. Like Go damn, it, everything's going to fall apart. I really messed this one up.
turns.zh: 尤其是当你身处其境时。比如天哪，一切都要崩盘了。我这次真的搞砸了。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And there's a trade-off with quality that people really struggle with. We've high standards of ourselves. A lot of Intercom comes from a design founder background. We value the craft a lot. We never want to be embarrassed by what we ship. So there's a real tension there, a real trade-off where people have these high standards, which we encourage and we encourage them to ship fast and learn and make mistakes. It's a constant kind of tension that we're navigating.
turns.zh: 是啊。在质量上也存在权衡，很多人为此纠结。我们对自己要求很高。在Intercom工作的很多人都有设计师背景，我们非常重视工艺。我们从不愿为自己推出的产品感到丢脸。因此，这里存在真正的矛盾，真正的权衡——人们有高标准，我们鼓励他们快速上线、快速学习、允许犯错。这是我们不断应对的矛盾局面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next up, we have Tom Conrad, who is chief product officer at Quibi and engineering leader at Pets.com. Two of the most memorable failures in product history, sharing his lessons from those wild experiences. Tom is currently CEO of Zero Longevity Science, which is a killer business and an app in case you haven't come across it. I'd definitely check it out. Here's Tom. (00:19:00): You brought up this phrase of notable disasters and I want to talk about that. You've worked at two of the most famous notable disasters of product companies, Pets.com and Quibi. I think it's really rare someone sees the inside of so much hype and then such a fall at a company. And so I just want to spend some time in these two areas, and maybe the way to set it up is just what's a lesson you took away from each of these two experiences that you've taken with you to future work, and maybe advice you share with people?
turns.zh: 接下来是汤姆·康拉德，他是Quibi的首席产品官，也是Pets.com的工程负责人。产品史上两个最令人难忘的失败案例，他将分享从这些疯狂经历中汲取的教训。汤姆目前是Zero Longevity Science的CEO，这是一家超棒的公司，还有一款应用，感兴趣的话可以去看看。我强烈推荐。汤姆，请上台。（00:19:00）你提到了“显著灾难”这个词，我想聊聊这个话题。你曾在两家最著名的产品公司——Pets.com和Quibi工作过，这两家都堪称产品界的典型灾难案例。很少有人能亲身经历如此热捧却又如此失败的公司历程。所以我想重点探讨这两个案例，或许先从你从这两次经历中汲取的教训说起，这些教训如何影响你未来的工作，以及你对他人的建议？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Probably the biggest lesson, it's not really about the specifics of the business. The biggest lesson really is these things make you better. In some instances, actually I think in both instances, they became kind of dominoes that opened doors for me in my own ambition and my own sort of professional life that maybe just wouldn't have opened at all if I hadn't gone to those companies and learned those things and had those experiences. And frankly, even in the case of Pets.com, like even the high profile nature of it, I could have worked at one of a thousand e-commerce websites in 1999. And when I went on to some subsequent job interview or something and talked about my experience, I had never heard of the thing that you worked on, but everybody certainly heard about Pets.com. (00:20:17): It's a pretty funny example too of how some struggles are timeless. That was 23, 24 years ago now. And while as a leadership team, we made, I'm sure, all kinds of mistakes. One of the things that happened was that there were three kind of over-funded pet e-commerce sites, and we all raised in excess of $50 million, which is a tremendous amount of money now. It was a tremendous amount of money then, and we all thought it was a zero-sum game and that we as one player started to spend on promotion or to spend irrationally on national broadcast television advertising. We all did, and it became this kind of unwinnable arms race. So there is, I think a fundamental lesson about having an excess of investment can be its own albatross or lead you to make decisions that maybe would be unwise. (00:21:28): And then of course, it's just like timing is really important. Chewy is a online pet store. It's worth $9 billion today. They were a private company and bought by PetSmart and then spun back out. But when they were bought by PetSmart, they were acquired for 3 billion, biggest e-commerce acquisition of all time. And while I think it's probably unfair to compare, Chewy who executed exceptionally well over a decade, grew their business brick by brick, and turned it into something really remarkable. To Pets.com, which was in a very, very different moment in time and tried to go to market in a really different way. (00:22:07): The critique that is often leveled at Pets.com or at least at the time, was like, this is just a stupid business. They're shipping dog food around. You could never make that work, and that's just wrong. You absolutely can make it work. Probably can't make it work when 80% of the country on the internet is still on dial up. It's really, really early.
turns.zh:
或许最重要的教训，并不在于业务的具体细节。真正重要的在于，这些经历能让你变得更强大。有些情况下，实际上在两种情况下，这些经历都像是多米诺骨牌，帮我打开了职业生涯的大门——如果没有去那些公司学习那些经验，这些机会或许根本不会降临。说实话，就连Pets.com的案例，尽管备受瞩目，但1999年我本可以选择千千万万家电商网站。后来参加面试时，我提及自己的经历，别人可能从未听说过你参与的项目，但所有人都知道Pets.com。（00:20:17）：这也是一个有趣的例子，说明有些困境是永恒的。那是23、24年前的事了。尽管作为管理团队，我们肯定犯过各种错误，但其中一个关键问题是，当时有三个资金过剩的宠物电商网站，我们每家都融资超过5000万美元——在当时这是一笔巨款。我们都认为这是一场零和博弈，当其中一家开始大肆投放推广广告或在全国性电视台做不理性的广告时，其他公司也纷纷效仿，最终陷入了不可取胜的军备竞赛。因此，我认为过剩的投资可能成为沉重的负担，导致决策失误。
（00:21:28）：当然，时机也至关重要。Chewy是一家在线宠物商店，如今估值90亿美元。他们曾是一家私营公司，被PetSmart收购后又被分拆上市。但被PetSmart收购时，他们的估值高达30亿美元，这是有史以来最大的电商收购案。虽然我觉得两者很难直接比较，但Chewy在过去十年里表现出色，一步一个脚印将业务做大，而Pets.com则处于完全不同的时代背景下，试图以截然不同的方式进入市场。
（00:22:07）：外界对Pets.com的批评——至少在当时——往往是"这就是个愚蠢的业务"、"他们只是在运送狗粮"、"这根本行不通"。但其实行得通。只是在80%的美国网民仍在使用拨号上网的时代，注定难以成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a stat I think you shared somewhere that you took Pets.com from nothing, to a public company, to completely out of business in 19 months.
turns.zh: 我记得你曾分享过数据，显示你们在19个月内就把Pets.com从无到有，发展成上市公司，最终又彻底倒闭。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, I think that's about right. The other thing that's forgotten in the tale is that we actually didn't go bankrupt. We shut the company down and returned the remaining balance to the investors, which no public company had ever done before. And the leadership team just reached the conclusion that given the way market conditions had evolved, there was just no way we were going to be able to get more capital into the company. And it was a company that required additional investment to get to profitability. And so it was better to wind down early, take the money that we had in the bank and get it back to investors than to just spend every last penny on what was sort of a fruitless attempt to salvage it.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。故事中被忽略的一点是，我们实际上并未破产。我们关闭了公司，将剩余资金返还给投资者，这在上市公司中前所未有。管理团队得出结论，鉴于市场环境变化，我们根本无法为公司筹集更多资金。而这家公司需要额外投资才能实现盈利。因此，早点结束业务、将银行存款返还投资者，比将最后一分钱用于徒劳的救助尝试要明智得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did not know that. Let's talk about Quibi. What went wrong there? Do you think there was a path to Quibi having worked out? Any big lessons that you took away from that experience that you bring with you?
turns.zh: 真不知道这回事。咱们来聊聊Quibi吧。它到底是哪儿出了问题？你觉得Quibi原本有可能成功吗？从这次经历中你有什么重要的收获和启发吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: The kind of miraculous thing about Quibi for me was it relit my enthusiasm for the industry for doing this work. I had left in, I think it was December of 2018, and I thought that maybe I was just done making software. I had done it for a really long time, I had done it for twenty-five years or something. And I had changed a lot. The industry had changed a lot, and I thought maybe I just didn't have the same passion for it that I had a decade before. And it also seemed like maybe it'd be fun to have another chapter of my life that was just completely different. And I had a whole list of things that I thought I might want to do. They were really, they were kind of ridiculous. Maybe I want to be a pastry chef. Maybe I want to be a landscape photographer. Maybe I want to learn to make bad music to put up on SoundCloud or something. Really the only thing they had in common were they were all things that I knew nothing about. People would be like, "Oh, you think you might want to be a pastry chef? Do you like to bake?" And I'd be like, "No, I don't know anything about baking." "Oh, you might landscape photography. Do you take photos?" "No, I don't make photos." (00:24:41): But I was kind of committed to the bit, actually to the point where when TechCrunch interviewed me about my departure from Snapchat, I was like, "I'm out. I'm going to do something else entirely." So that story is very much out there. But a few months after my last day at Snap, I got a call from Meg Whitman and Jeffrey Katzenberg who were starting up, it was called New TV at the time. (00:25:07): And the pitch was, "We're going to try to take the best of mobile and Silicon Valley and Consumer Tech and sort of weld it to the best of Hollywood-style content production to build something completely bespoke and purpose-made for consumption on the phone." They were looking for both technology leadership and product leadership and wanted to know if I was interested in one or both. And I took the meeting, even though I wasn't really taking these kinds of calls from anybody. It just seemed like who's going to pass up the opportunity to have lunch with the two of them? So I listened to the pitch and politely declined and told them that I was going to be a pastry chef or something. And we kept doing that every couple of months for seven months. We'd go to lunch, they would give me an update on the progress they were making, and I would decline the invitation to get involved somehow. (00:26:05): And then late in that year, I went to lunch one more time and Meg explained that they brought on someone to lead technology and they brought another person to lead product, and both of them really truly for reasons that are completely disconnected from Quibi itself, both of them had left after about six weeks. And Meg's like, "We've raised all this money, and we've told the world that we're shipping this product in about a year. We got an awful lot to do, and I really could use some help, and I would consider it a personal favor if you would come and spend just a couple of days a week helping." She's like, "I'll continue to look for someone who actually wants the job, but it'd be great if you could help me get this off the ground." (00:26:53): And my wife is a freelance writer, marketing strategist and loves her life as a freelance contributor. And she's like, "You should do this. Why not? It's two days a week, it's just a few months. What's the worst thing that could happen? Maybe you'll like it." And I'm like, "No, no. Here's the thing that will happen. I won't do it two days a week. It will immediately be three days, then four days, then five days, then six days. I just know myself." And she's like, "No." She's like, "Just on Wednesday night at six o'clock, close your Quibi laptop and be like, all they're paying me for is for Tuesday and Wednesday and then open it back up on Tuesday morning. That's all you've got to do." (00:27:35): Well, she's right about most things and she's wrong about this. I fell deeply into it right away, and it was just so fun to get to build a team from scratch and to design and build a product from scratch and to take advantage of all of the sort of modern software architecture stuff that had come into being over the course of the 15 years since we had started Pandora. And I'm embarrassed about some of the what happened with Quibi for sure, but I'm super grateful for the experience, because I just really fell in love with the industry again and was reminded of just how rewarding it can be to build something and to try to put it out there even if you stumble pretty mightily along the way.
turns.zh:
对我来说，Quibi最神奇的地方在于，它重新点燃了我对这个行业的热情，让我重燃了做这份工作的激情。2018年12月，我离开了之前的公司，当时我以为自己可能已经结束了软件开发生涯。毕竟我在这个领域深耕了25年，行业也发生了巨大变化，我发现自己对这份工作的热情已不如从前。当时我还想，或许是时候开启人生的新篇章，尝试完全不同的领域。于是我列了一长串可能想做的事——有些想法甚至很荒谬，比如成为糕点师、风景摄影师、在SoundCloud上发布音乐作品等等。但这些想法的共同点就是，我对它们一无所知。别人会问：“哦，你想当糕点师？你会烘焙吗？”我回答：“不，我对烘焙一窍不通。”“你想当风景摄影师？你会拍照吗？”我回答：“不，我根本不拍照。”（00:24:41）但我当时确实下了决心，甚至在TechCrunch采访我离开Snapchat的经历时，坦言：“我要彻底离开，去做些完全不同的事。”这段故事广为人知。但离开Snapchat几个月后，梅格·惠特曼和杰夫·卡岑伯格邀请我加入他们当时名为New TV的初创公司。（00:25:07）他们的构想是：“我们要将移动科技、硅谷精神和消费科技的精华与好莱坞式的内容制作相结合，打造专为手机端量身打造的独特体验。” 他们既需要技术领导力，也需要产品领导力，询问我是否有兴趣加入其中一个或两个团队。尽管我当时并不常接这种电话，但想想看，和这两位共进午餐的机会，谁能拒绝呢？于是我听完他们的提案后，礼貌地拒绝了，说自己要去当糕点师之类的。这样的对话持续了七个月，每隔几个月就见面吃午餐。他们会汇报进展，我每次都以各种借口拒绝参与其中。（00:26:05）直到那年年底，我再去吃一次午餐，梅格解释说他们请了技术和产品负责人，但两人都因为与Quibi无关的原因，在六周后离职了。梅格说：“我们筹集了这么多资金，还向全世界宣称一年内上线产品。现在任务繁重，我真的需要帮助。如果你能每周来帮忙几天，那真是帮大忙了。” 她说：“我会继续寻找真正想做这份工作的人，但如果你能帮我启动项目，我会感激不尽。” （00:26:53）我的妻子是一名自由撰稿人、营销策略师，热爱自由职业的生活。她说：“你应该试试看。为什么不呢？每周两天，就几个月的事。最坏能怎样呢？说不定你会喜欢上它的。” 我回答：“不，不。关键是，我不会每周来两天的。”
接下来会是三天，然后四天，再然后五天，最后六天。我太了解自己了。” 她说：“不行。” 她说：“就周三晚上六点关掉你的Quibi笔记本电脑，然后想想，他们付钱给我的是周二和周三的费用，周二早上再重新打开它。就这么简单。” （00:27:35）：嗯，她大部分说得对，但这件事她错了。我一下子就深陷其中了，能从零开始组建团队，设计和开发产品，充分利用我们自从创办Pandora以来15年间涌现的各种现代软件架构技术，这真是太有趣了。对于Quibi的遭遇，我确实感到有些尴尬，但我非常感激这段经历，因为我再次爱上了这个行业，也再次意识到创造出一些东西并将其推向市场是多么有意义的事情，即便过程中会遇到重重挫折。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something that you took away from that experience that taught you what to try to avoid, to try to pull towards?
turns.zh: 通过那次经历，你是否学到了一些东西，让你明白应该避免做什么、努力去追求什么呢？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I think I sort of misunderstood or misjudged companies sometimes by thinking about them really focused on the product execution. If you find an interesting problem that people care about and you solve that problem in a really beautiful, elegant, delightful way, that's 10 times better than anything else that they can get in that same space, they'll tell their friends and all the rest will take care of itself. And so that was always my ambition. Find a thing that I cared about building, do a great job building it in a delightful way, go really deep on listening to people and their feedback and iterate your way to success and breaking through that membrane that we all strive to get across, the really great word of mouth. (00:29:27): But I think the thing I've come to better appreciate is that companies are also, they're kind of a math problem that describes how you take investment and pour them into the equation, and out the other side comes returns on some time horizon. And yes, there are variables in that equation that are influenced by the product that you build and all of the little details and decisions that you make about making that product great. But if the equation is fundamentally broken or a big swing in and of itself, no amount of iteration and execution can get you out of the failed outputs of the broken equation. (00:30:14): And I think Quibi made a bet that you could build an entirely bespoke content library that was sufficiently scaled to get people to subscribe and retain for a couple billion dollars. It was a huge amount of money, but we made 70 shows in 18 months, which is more content than all of the major broadcast networks combined made in a single year. So it was a pretty major accomplishment. And we made a bet that we would augment those sort of episodic and serialized or Hollywood style shows with a bunch of daily content that we produce at the level of network television, nightly news, and so forth that would be an alternative to some of the sort of daily content that you might otherwise get on YouTube. And that was going to be about a third of the content spend. (00:31:19): One super interesting thing that no one talks about is that all of that content was designed to be made day of or day before it aired. So there was no back catalog of it, and it was all designed to be shot in these professional studios that we built out, and it was really expensive. Like I said, it was a third of the investment we were going to make in content, almost half the investment we were going to be making content. And we launched two weeks into Covid, and we couldn't make any of that content except literally in the garages of the host's homes. And so we had this thing that was supposed to seem really set apart from YouTube that literally now was being made exactly YouTube content, which is sort of like self-produced at home with very little sort of the support infrastructure of Hollywood. (00:32:10): Now you can argue, I think the content on YouTube is really, really exceptional in this category, and maybe we were never going to do better than that. But I think what was really fundamentally broken with Quibi was that the actual foundational equation of can you make enough premium content that's totally bespoke and made for the service and takes advantage of the nature of the phone, is that enough content to get people to sign up and retain, and can you do that for a couple billion dollars? And I think the answer is no. The library has to be much, much bigger and you have to have, like any company, you have to have sufficient time and energy to iterate on the content format itself. Our roadmap really wanted to innovate on the content format. And so I think part of what happened is pretty quickly it became clear that the math was just wrong. It wasn't going to take 2 billion, it was going to take six or eight or 10 billion. And the risk reward profile of betting 10 billion on the format was just more than anyone can stomach.
turns.zh:
我觉得自己有时会误解或错误判断一些公司，总是认为它们过于专注于产品执行。若你能发现一个人们关心的有趣问题，并以极其美妙、优雅、令人愉悦的方式解决它，这比同领域其他产品好十倍。人们会把它推荐给朋友，其余的自然水到渠成。这始终是我的抱负——找到一个我热衷于打造的产品，以卓越的方式完成开发，深入倾听用户反馈，通过迭代实现成功，突破我们都渴望突破的壁垒——口碑传播。（00:29:27）但我现在越发意识到，公司本质上也是一个数学方程式：如何将投资注入等式，经过一段时间后获得回报。诚然，这个方程式中的变量会受到你所打造的产品、以及为优化产品而做出的诸多决策的影响。但若方程式本身存在根本性缺陷，或因某个变量剧烈波动，再多的迭代与执行也无法摆脱失败的结果。（00:30:14）Quibi曾押注于打造一个完全定制的内容库，通过规模化内容吸引用户订阅，投资金额高达数十亿美元。这笔巨额资金投入下，我们在18个月内制作了70部节目，内容量超过所有主流广播电视网一年产量总和。这确实是一项重大成就。我们计划用网络电视级别的每日新闻等内容，补充那些分集式、连载式或好莱坞风格的节目，替代YouTube上的日常内容。这部分内容将占据约三分之一的节目支出。（00:31:19）一个极为有趣却鲜少被提及的细节是，所有内容都是在播出前一天或当天完成制作的。没有任何存档内容，所有拍摄都在我们搭建的专业影棚完成，成本极高。正如我所言，这笔投资本应用于内容创作，实际却占了投资的近半数。我们在新冠疫情爆发两周后上线，却只能在主持人自家车库完成拍摄。我们本想打造与YouTube截然不同的产品，结果却沦为低成本、缺乏好莱坞式支持基础设施的自制内容。（00:32:10）或许有人会说，YouTube的相关内容确实卓越超群，或许我们本就无法超越。但Quibi的根本问题在于：能否打造出完全为平台量身定制、充分利用手机特性的优质内容？这些内容能否吸引用户订阅并留存？以数十亿美元的投入能否实现这一目标？答案显然是否定的。内容库必须规模宏大，且像任何公司一样，需要足够的筹备时间。
以及投入精力和资源来优化内容格式本身。我们的路线图确实希望在内容格式方面有所创新。但我认为部分问题在于，很快就发现我们的计算严重失误了。实际所需资金不止20亿，而是60亿、80亿、100亿。把100亿资金押注在这种内容格式上，其风险回报比实在超出了任何人的承受范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next up, we've got Sri Batchu, former head of growth at Ramp who shares something that I've thought about ever since we had this conversation, which is this idea that when you fail, make sure you fail conclusively to make this failure an actual learning that you can build off of versus just a waste of time. Here's Sri.
turns.zh: 接下来，是Ramp公司前增长部门主管Sri Batchu的分享。他提出的观点让我深有共鸣：当你遭遇失败时，必须确保失败是彻底的，这样才能将这份教训转化为真正的成长动能，而非徒劳的试错。现在请听听Sri的见解。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Growth experiments in my history are typically like 30%-ish success rate. So the vast majority of things that you try don't work. And so you want to create a culture where people aren't afraid to take risks and aren't afraid to fail. And for me, failure is not that you didn't drive revenue, failure is not learning. So it's really important that you learn when you fail. And so we celebrate failure as long as you're learning, and you can only learn if you've designed the right test and you failed conclusively, because otherwise I think many of us have been in situations where there's intuition that something might work and it doesn't work, and then you end up doing it over and over for years because every time a new executive or somebody else has the same idea, you try it again. And it's because you haven't been able to design the test to fail conclusively. (00:34:31): It's hard to do. But at the end of the day, there's only two ways to make an experiment successful. Either you have a very large M or you have a very significant treatment, which is what you're doing in the experiment itself. And in B2B, you don't usually have the luxury of large M, which you [inaudible 00:34:54] consumer. (00:34:54): Facebook can get [inaudible 00:34:56] in two hours. A B2B company could take two years to get to the same number of touch points. And so to counteract that, I recommend people just trying to maximize the treatment effect, which is like if you have a hypothesis that you're testing, just throw all of the possible tactics and resources that you think would move that needle because you can always cost rationalize later if it works. (00:35:22): And so just maximize the treatment effect. And if with all of that it didn't work, then you can say, "Hey, we're not going to try this again because we literally did try everything that we could to test this hypothesis. And if it doesn't work in the best version, and it's expensive as it is, this is not worth spending more time on." But if it does work, great. Then you do another version of the test with half the tactics or whichever tactics you think work better or worse and you optimize over time.
turns.zh:
回顾我的增长实验史，成功率通常只有30%左右。这意味着绝大多数尝试都以失败告终。因此，我们需要营造一种文化，让人们敢于冒险、敢于失败。对我而言，失败并非指未能创造收入，而是未能从中汲取教训。所以关键在于失败后要及时总结经验。只要能从失败中学习，我们就应当为失败喝彩。但只有当测试设计得当、失败结果明确时，学习才真正发生。否则，许多人会陷入误区——凭直觉认为某个策略有效却徒劳尝试，因为他们未能设计出能明确验证假设的测试。

（00:34:31）：这很难做到。但归根结底，成功实验的关键在于两点：要么有极大的市场规模，要么有显著的实验干预力度。这正是B2B领域的痛点——我们通常没有消费品领域那样的规模优势。（00:34:54）：Facebook可能在两小时内完成测试，而B2B公司可能需要两年才能达到相同的触达量。因此，我建议企业全力优化实验效果：针对假设，动用所有可能的策略和资源进行验证。若效果不佳，再进行成本核算。（00:35:22）：最大化实验效果后，若仍未成功，就可以果断放弃：“我们不会再尝试了，因为我们已竭尽全力验证假设。若最佳版本都失败且成本高昂，就不值得继续投入。” 但若成功了，再优化策略，逐步提升效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example you could share when you did that?
turns.zh: 你能分享一个这样的成功案例吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Account-based marketing is something that is very common in enterprise software where you've selected certain customers that you think are high priority and you're saying, "I want to touch them in as many nuanced ways possible to see if that drives conversion." And this is something I've seen tried many times where people do it, but they kind of do it halfway where they're like, okay, tried these three things. Conversion of the control group wasn't higher, and so we think it is not going to work. And then a new go-to-market executive comes and they have to do it again. They have to do it again. They have to do it again. It's like a very common one wherever this happens. And so when we did it at Ramp, we did exactly what I just described, which is like, let's really be thoughtful about the experiment design, both in terms of maximizing the number of people as well as maximizing the number of ways and types of ways that we're effectively touching these target customers to show the value one way or the other.
turns.zh:
基于账户的营销在企业软件领域非常常见。企业会选定一些认为优先级较高的客户，试图通过尽可能多样化的方式接触这些客户，以观察是否能提升转化率。我曾多次见证这样的尝试，但多数人做得半途而废，比如尝试了三种方法后，发现对照组的转化率没有提升，就认为策略无效。然后新上任的市场营销高管又得重新来过。这类失败案例屡见不鲜。

在Ramp公司，我们采取了精心设计的实验方案：首先，尽可能扩大实验规模，尝试多种有效接触目标客户的方式，以验证其价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what it sounds like is the hypothesis isn't like this email will have a big impact on conversion. It's like this strategy of coming after customers is what we're testing.
turns.zh: 听起来关键点不在于这封邮件是否能显著提升转化率，而是我们正在测试这种主动触达客户的策略。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: That's the example there. And I think for example, if you had the... This kind of framework is more important for cross-functional, larger scale, bigger tests rather than an email modification. But we can even use it on a micro example like an email modification where you are like, "Okay, I think this particular email is underperforming because it's not talking to this part of the customer's pain point or journey or what have you." And you could just, the simplest test would be, okay, let me make some tweaks to the text and edit that, and that could be the end of that test. And if that doesn't work, you're like, "Oh, maybe those weren't the right text edits. Let me do a different text edits or whatever." (00:38:02): And that's fine, that's low cost. It's not the end of the world and it's for you to be wrong there. But an alternative that you could do is like, "Oh, what are all of the things that I could change about this email in the same test?" Is it the trigger of the email? Is it the text content of the email? Is it additional personalization? Is it the design of the email? Trying to think of what are all of the various levers that you think could be wrong and put them all together to test your hypothesis of this touch point is wrong, and how do I improve that?
turns.zh: 这里举个例子。这种框架对于跨职能、大规模测试更为重要，而非单纯的邮件优化。但即使是邮件优化这样的微观案例，我们也能应用这一思路。比如，当你发现某封邮件表现不佳时，可能归因于它未能触及客户的痛点、用户旅程等核心需求。此时，最简单的方法就是调整文案内容，但如果效果不佳，再尝试其他修改。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, obviously the downside of that is you, if it doesn't work, you don't know if it's like, oh, maybe it was this thing could have worked in the subject.
turns.zh: 当然，失败的代价不算太高，但总归要承认自己的错误。另一种替代方案是：列出邮件可能存在问题的各个维度——触发机制、文案内容、个性化程度、设计风格等——并整合所有变量来验证假设是否错误，以及如何改进。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, so there's always trade-offs on this, but what you're hoping is you've done a complete refresh where you did all the things that you thought were intuitive that should work. And if it doesn't work, then you're like, okay, maybe my hypothesis wrong. But you're right. There's always going to be a challenge if maybe the execution is wrong. And I did too many things potentially in that case.
turns.zh: 当然，失败后你无法确定问题出在标题上，还是其他环节。但总归要权衡利弊。理想情况是，你完成了全面的优化，尝试了所有直觉上有效的方案。如果还是不行，那就承认假设错误。但有时候可能是执行环节出了问题，我自己就曾在这种情况下犯过太多错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Our next story is from JZ, who is a colleague of mine at Airbnb, head of product at Webflow when we recorded this episode, and this is her sharing the story of one of the biggest product misses at Airbnb. (00:39:13): You've seen a lot of new PMs, and you've seen these PMs succeed, you've seen some fail. What are the most common mistakes that you find new PMs make in this experience of helping new PMs get into the field? Jiaona Zhang (JZ) (00:39:27): I think something that is really hard to untrain, but I think every human does it, is you jump to solutions. And so one of the biggest things I see, not just in my course, but also just as a PM and some of the mistakes that you make as a PM is the idea of you get really attached to a solution, a way of implementing something, something that you can see in your head that you want to build. And so that's the first thing I really want to like unteach in our course. (00:39:50): And so a lot of people will literally come in, they'll be like, "I want to build X startup," or, "I want to do this thing," or, "I am in blank school, and I've been doing a lot of research on this particular area." And so untraining that and being like, "Hey, we're going to go out there. We are not going to think at all about the thing that you want to build, but instead we're going to be focused on users and people in the real world and their problems. And the first step is to understand their problems and then understand if there's an opportunity here as opposed to, hey, you want to build X thing for Y person." So that's the biggest mistake that you really have to unteach and retrain thinking around.
turns.zh:
我们的下一位嘉宾是JZ，她是我在Airbnb的同事，在录制本期节目时担任Webflow的产品负责人。她将分享Airbnb史上最严重的产品失败案例之一。  
（00:39:13）：你见过很多新晋产品经理，他们有的成功了，也有的失败了。在帮助新晋产品经理入行的过程中，你发现他们最常犯的错误是什么？  
张娇娜（JZ）（00:39:27）：我认为有一种很难改掉的习惯，但几乎每个人都会犯，那就是急于寻找解决方案。在我的课程中，我发现最常见的错误之一，也是我作为产品经理常犯的错误，就是过度执着于某个解决方案、某种实施方式，或者某个你脑海中构想的功能。这是我在课程中最想纠正的第一个问题。  
（00:39:50）：很多新人一进来就会说：“我想创办X类初创公司”，或者“我想做这个项目”，或者“我在某某学校学习过，针对这个领域做了大量研究”。但我们需要纠正这种思维，告诉他们：“我们要先深入了解用户和现实世界中的人们所面临的问题，而不是一开始就想着要开发什么功能。首先要理解用户的痛点，然后再判断是否有可行的商业机会，而不是一开始就执着于‘为某类用户打造X功能’。” 这才是最需要纠正和重新培养思维模式的关键误区。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's go to the other side of this question. We talked about what mistakes new PMs make. I'm curious, what's the biggest product mistake that you've made? Jiaona Zhang (JZ) (00:40:34): Wow, that's a good one. It's so interesting. I feel like as product people we're always making mistakes and we're always learning. Maybe I'll give an example from Airbnb since you and I were both there. (00:40:43): And this one does stand out to me. So we're working on this concept called Airbnb Plus. If you took a step back, what we're really trying to do is to be like, "Hey, not everyone trusts Airbnb in terms of it's a platform. It's not like it's managed inventory, it's not a hotel. How do you go in and really make sure that we're all the Airbnbs are meeting the quality bar?" But I do think we were very solution first, and I think we're also competitor afraid at the time. So it was during a time where there were managed marketplaces, there were the Saunders out there, and I think that as a company we're very much like, "Oh, look at this. What are we going to do in the world of managed marketplaces?" (00:41:19): And so we went really hard down the solution space. We essentially were like, "Let's go inspect our inventory. Let's actually try to manage our inventory more." And really what we should have done is taken a step back and be like, "What's the real problem?" The real problem is people want to know what they're getting themselves into. We need to represent the homes a lot better. And I think the other piece here that's really important is what, as a company, is there strategic strength? And what's in your wheelhouse? So for example, Airbnb, we weren't that strong in operations. We again, we're this platform with this marketplace. And so if you don't have that muscle and then you're asking the company, the teams to essentially build it from the ground up, that's really, really difficult. Not to mention the unit economics. Are the unit economics actually going to work, even as you scale?
turns.zh: 接下来让我们来探讨这个问题的另一面。我们刚刚讨论了新任产品经理常犯的错误。那么，我很好奇，你们犯过的最严重的产品决策失误是什么？张佳诺（JZ）（00:40:34）：哇，这个问题问得真好。这太有意思了。作为产品从业者，我们似乎总是在犯错，也总是在不断学习。或许我可以举个Airbnb的例子，毕竟你我都曾在那里工作过。（00:40:43）：这个例子确实让我印象深刻。当时我们正在开发一个叫做“Airbnb Plus”的项目。退一步来说，我们真正想解决的问题是：“嘿，不是所有人都信任Airbnb这个平台的。它毕竟不是集中管理库存的酒店，也不是传统酒店。如何确保所有房源都能达到高质量标准呢？” 但我认为当时我们过于急于找到解决方案，同时也对竞争对手心存恐惧。当时市面上有不少集中管理的平台，比如Saunders这样的竞争对手。我记得公司内部当时都在想：“天，看看这个竞争对手。我们该如何在集中管理的平台领域中立足呢？” 于是我们一头扎进解决方案的开发中。我们当时的思路是：“先去检查我们的房源库存，再尝试加强库存管理。” 但其实我们本该退一步，问问自己：“真正的问题是什么？” 真正的问题是用户需要明确了解他们即将入住的房源情况。我们需要更好地展示房源信息。另外一个关键点在于，Airbnb作为一家平台型公司，战略优势何在？哪些业务是我们的核心专长？比如说，在运营能力方面，Airbnb当时并不强。我们毕竟只是一个平台型公司，缺乏必要的执行能力。如果要从零开始搭建这些能力体系，难度实在太大了。更何况还有单位经济效益的考量。即便规模化之后，单位经济效益能否真正可行？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I feel like Airbnb Plus is an untold story that somebody should tell, and that could be its own podcast, I guess. Jiaona Zhang (JZ) (00:42:09): You and I can tell it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得Airbnb Plus的故事值得深入挖掘，或许可以单独做一期播客来讲讲。张佳诺（JZ）（00:42:09）：你我可以一起来分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We could tell it. This could be Airbnb Plus the hidden, the story. As you said, the problem it was trying to solve was people don't really trust, they don't want to even consider Airbnb. Like, "No, I don't want to stay in someone's home. I don't know what it'll be. It's unpredictable." And so as an outsider, it felt like a really clever approach. We're going to get them, we're going to make sure they're awesome. There's a minimum bar. And I guess this is the question is do you think it was just like this is never possible because we'll never make money as a business doing this, because we don't make that much booking and investing time, resources, sending people pillows, all that stuff is ever going to be economical. Or do you think there was a path, and it was just not executed well? Jiaona Zhang (JZ) (00:42:51): I think there wasn't really a clear path. I think there was [inaudible 00:42:55]. Exactly. And it was more just like if you understood, again, this is my point around unit economics, there are things where I think you have magical thinking around unit economics. You're like, "Well, when we get to the scale of X, it's all going to work out. We can make these things happen." I think you actually need to really make sure the unit economics work right at the beginning. So that is definitely one lesson. (00:43:14): And I think the other thing is, and going back to the spirit of what are you trying to achieve. If you're trying to achieve this idea of really knowing the quality of the place, and for a platform like Airbnb, the right way to go about doing is through our reviews, through our guest reviews, which are essentially free as opposed to literally sending out inspectors. (00:43:32): And I think that the other things are if you can get signal on what are the things around quality that people care about? Is it cleaning? Is it the, "Hey, I'm locked out." And I think that there are other solutions besides inspection that then get at that. So for example, it is actually cheaper to go send everyone a lockbox than to deploy an inspector and go look at your property, right? It is actually cheaper to maybe do a partnership with a bunch of cleaners in different local areas, and then get that as part of the feat as opposed to doing inspection. (00:44:04): So again, it's really about what are you really trying to achieve? What is the user problem in each of these areas, and can you target that problem with the particular listing that you're looking at? And so yeah, I personally don't believe the unit economics ever would've really worked out. I think we should have known that, or we should have dug into that more at the very beginning, and then to get very tailored instead of one blunt instrument to solve it all. Hey, we're going to go inspect. It's like, what is the problem for this listing, and what's the best solution to fix that problem?
turns.zh: 吉娅娜·张（JZ）（00:42:51）：我认为当时并没有一个清晰的路径。我觉得（观众）当时的想法是，"嗯，我们需要先把产品做好，然后再考虑其他问题。"但问题是，Airbnb Plus 的成功路径根本不清晰。（00:43:14）我认为最重要的是，要确保单位经济模型从一开始就行得通。（00:43:32）另外，用户真正关心的质量问题是什么呢？是清洁问题？还是“我被锁在门外了”这样的情况？除了派检查员去实地考察，难道没有其他解决方案吗？比如，给所有房东发一个智能锁，成本会低很多吧？（00:44:04）所以关键在于，你要清楚自己的目标用户是谁，每个用户的痛点是什么，以及如何通过具体的房源信息来精准解决问题。（00:44:14）总之，关键在于，你要确保单位经济模型从一开始就可行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Our second to last story is from Gina Gotthilf, who was an early growth leader at Duolingo. She's currently COO of Latitud, and this is her sharing a wide-ranging and important point about how everyone has both an A side and a B side to their career, and people often only share their A side. So this is Gina sharing her B side.
turns.zh: 我们的倒数第二个故事来自杜绝学的早期增长负责人吉娅娜·戈特希尔夫。她目前是 Latitud 的首席运营官。在这个故事中，她分享了一个广泛而重要的观点：每个人的职业生涯都有正面和负面两面，而人们往往只分享正面的一面。接下来就让我们听听吉娅娜如何分享她的负面经历。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: We are very encouraged in our lives, especially professionally, to talk about our A side all the time because that's what impresses people. That's what opens doors, that's what allows us to keep growing, and it's so important. So it means that a lot of what you hear in podcasts and on stage ends up being the Instagramable version of someone or a company or a country's trajectory. It's just the highlights. And when I talk about my A side, it's very impressive. I did things like, we'll talk about, I met President Obama, I worked on the Mike Bloomberg presidential campaign. I helped Duolingo scale from three to 200 million users. I worked with Tumblr, helping them scale Latin America, Andreesen Horowitz invested in my company, etc. (00:45:34): But between all of those highlights, there were so many B moments that get shoved under the rug because it's just easier for me and it's more impressive for others. But I really like to highlight those because I think that most of us have a lot of B moments every day, every week, every month, and every period of our lives. And it's easy to think that things aren't just not going to work out for us because we're in one of those B moments if we don't recognize them as moments.
turns.zh: 我们的生活中——尤其是职场场合——常被鼓励时刻展现自己的亮点，因为这能给人留下深刻印象，助我们打开机遇之门，推动个人成长。这非常重要。因此，播客节目和演讲台上呈现的多是某人、某公司或某国发展历程的精华版——全是高光时刻。谈及我的个人经历时，确实有很多亮点：比如，我曾与奥巴马总统会面，为迈克·布隆伯格的总统竞选团队工作过，帮助多邻国用户量从300万增长至2亿，助力Tumblr在拉丁美洲扩张，安德森·霍洛维茨曾投资我的公司等等（00:45:34）。 但在这些高光时刻背后，还有许多被忽视的低谷时刻。这些时刻被我刻意掩盖，只因它们不易被他人理解，却承载着我日常生活中的真实缩影。若不正视这些低谷，我们很容易陷入自我怀疑，认为事情注定失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this concept. We're going to talk as you expected about a lot of your A side stuff. Is there any example of a B side story of your life that would be interesting to share?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个概念。正如你所期待的，我们会聊聊你人生中的诸多亮点。但你是否有过有趣的低谷故事，愿意分享呢？

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Look, I think those are the most interesting because they're funny or ridiculous. I had a lot of B sides, and I still do. For example, I had no idea what I wanted to do. I actually wanted to be. I thought I wanted to be an actress. I either wanted to be that person in Sea World, who goes like this with a dolphin. This is before Sea World was canceled. Or I wanted to be an actress. I applied to schools. I didn't get into any Ivy League. I didn't get into any of the top schools I wanted to go to. When I got to college, I actually ended up dropping out because I got so depressed, incredibly depressed, couldn't get out of bed depressed. Ironically, I dropped out of Reed College, which is the same college that Steve Jobs dropped out of. So I was just destined for greatness. I knew it at that moment.
turns.zh: 说实话，这些低谷故事最引人入胜——因为它们既搞笑又荒诞。我曾经历过许多低谷时刻，现在依然如此。比如，我曾一度迷茫未来方向，曾想当演员，甚至模仿海洋世界里与海豚互动的场景（那还是海洋世界被曝光前的事）。申请大学时，没能进入常春藤盟校或心仪的顶尖学府。大学期间因抑郁症辍学，简直卧床不起。讽刺的是，我就读的里德学院正是史蒂夫·乔布斯曾就读的学校——看来我注定要成就非凡。当时我深信不疑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It all makes sense looking backwards, as he said.
turns.zh: 正如他所说，事后看来，诸多曲折皆成铺垫。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Totally. I was dropping out, being like, "Yes, this is exactly the path." No, I was miserable. I thought there was no path forward. And I finally went back and graduated. The college counselor looked at my curriculum and said, "What have you even done with your life? There's nothing to show for." And it was shocking because I was always the overachiever who wants to do the maximum curriculum and ace all of my classes and do whatever. I did three diplomas in high school, the international, the American, the Brazilian. (00:47:22): And so that for me, I think my one learning there that has stuck with me, and I think it can work for other people too, is that it's not just about doing things that actually matter and learning. It's about being able to tell the story, and it's about understanding what other people perceive as valuable. I applied to a hundred companies. I didn't hear back from most of them. I finally got an internship at kind a tier B/C digital marketing agency in New York City because I wanted to live in New York so badly. And they forgot to apply for my visa on time. So I lost my visa and had to go back to Brazil, and then I ended up leaving that organization to go work for another one. And I won't even go into the details of the shadiness of that company that I worked for, but then they ended up laying me off. So I lost my visa again, had to go back home, found another opportunity, got fired that time. So there was just a lot of rockiness in my start that I don't think you would imagine when you see someone up on stage leading a conference for 5,000 people. That I think is important. (00:48:26): And even when I started working for Tumblr, I was like, "This is it. I made it. This is a really interesting company. This is going to work out." That was super rocky because it was an early stage startup. So for example, they couldn't figure out how to wire money to Brazil. So I was not paid for six months. And at one point, me and my colleagues were trying to get money out of the teller to pay contractors because we had no money to pay them, and we borrowed money from people. And finally they also laid me off because they decided to sell to Yahoo. (00:48:54): And then I had to figure out what am I going to do? No one's going to hire me. I've been fired and laid off so many times. So this is all before I started an agency to help US-based tech companies and startups grow in Latin America because I figured I was in this really great place to make that happen. And it eventually worked for, well-known companies such as Duolingo. At the time they weren't well-known. They were a tiny little startup. They didn't have an Android app. And that's how I started working with Duolingo because their head of marketing connected with someone they had worked with at Flickr and said, "I noticed Tumblr grew a lot in Brazil last year. Can you recommend a company or an agency to help?" And they said, "This girl." And I was twenty-six. And so that's how they connected me with Duolingo. And I started helping them grow in Brazil as a consultant. They were like, "This is great. Can you help us grow in Chile, Argentina?" And I was like, "Yes." They were like, "How about Mexico?" And I was like, "Yes." Did I know anything about these places, Lenny? Did I know people there? No, but you can figure it out. (00:49:51): And then they ended up asking me to come on full time, do that across the world, Japan, China, Korea, Turkey, Spain, France, et cetera. And then to own growth, which ended up meaning communications, social media, government partnerships, anything to grow. And then eventually became an A/B testing growth engine with engineers and PMs and designers of which I knew nothing about. (00:50:15): And even after that, I left Duolingo five years later, didn't know what to do with my life. You'd think, "Oh wow, you have it figured out now. You left Duolingo, you have the world in front of you." And I'm like, "Maybe I can finally go work for nonprofits," which is what I actually wanted to do in the first place. Tried a hand at that. Had a couple of experiences before going to work for the Mike Bloomberg campaign. (00:50:36): Working for the Mike Bloomberg campaign is impressive. But you know what? Mike Bloomberg didn't win. He's not the president. So that was not a successful campaign if you really look at it. And yeah, Latitud seems like it's a really promising path, but there's A days and B days. So it's just a lot of that. And just staying resilient and believing in yourself and getting back on the horse when you fall on your face.
turns.zh:
完全正确。我当时差点退学，心想：“没错，这就是我该走的路。”但实际上我过得一团糟，觉得前路迷茫。最后我还是回去完成了学业。大学辅导员看着我的课程表问：“你这辈子都做了什么？一无是处！” 这让我很震惊，因为我一直是那种想要把课程学到极致、门门功课都拿A、事事都尽力做到最高的优等生。高中时我修了三个文凭——国际文凭、美国文凭和巴西文凭。（00:47:22）对我来说，最重要的学习启示是，成功不止于做有意义的事和学习，还在于能把经历讲清楚，理解别人眼中珍视的东西。我申请了上百家公司，大部分没收到回复。最后我在纽约一家二、三线数字营销公司实习，因为我太想去纽约了。结果他们忘了按时申请我的签证，我因此失去签证被迫回巴西，接着又跳槽到另一家公司。但那家公司极不靠谱，最后还裁员，我又丢了签证。这些挫折超乎你想象，当你看到台上领奖的5000人时根本想不到幕后故事。这很重要。（00:48:26）甚至加入Tumblr时，我也以为：“就是这样了，我成功了。这家公司超棒，一定行。”但那时它还是初创公司，问题多多。比如，他们不知道怎么给巴西汇款，我六个月没领到工资。有一回我和同事想从银行取钱支付合作伙伴工资，因为实在没钱了，还向别人借钱。最后公司被雅虎收购，又裁员了。（00:48:54）我不得不重新找路。但没人愿意雇我，屡遭裁员。于是我创办公司，帮助美国科技公司和初创企业在拉美发展。我发现自己身处绝佳位置。最终合作了Duolingo。当时它还名不见经传，刚起步，没有安卓版应用。我就是通过Flickr的市场总监推荐才接到合作的。
任何能让我成长的机会都行。而最终，我加入了一个由工程师、产品经理和设计师组成的A/B测试增长团队——这些领域我之前一无所知。（00:50:15）即便如此，五年后我离开了Duolingo，却依然不知道自己该何去何从。你可能会想：“哇，你现在终于找到了方向。离开Duolingo后，整个世界都为你敞开了。” 但我却在想：“或许我终于能去非营利组织工作了”——这毕竟是我最初就想做的事。我尝试过，但在加入迈克·布隆伯格竞选团队之前，只积累了些许经验。（00:50:36）为迈克·布隆伯格竞选团队工作固然令人钦佩，但说实话，他没能胜选，也没当上总统。所以从结果来看，这场竞选并不算成功。拉丁图（Latitud）似乎是一条很有前景的道路，但也会有顺境和逆境。关键在于保持韧性，相信自己，跌倒了就重新站起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That's such an important message. I think one of the threads from what you're describing, something that I think about a lot is people kind of underestimate how long their career is. There's just so much time to do stuff and for things to start to work. This going to sound really fancy, but I think Marcus Aurelius has this quote about how our life is actually very long. We just use it really badly and we just waste a lot of our time.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是条重要启示。我觉得你所说的核心观点之一，也是我常深思的问题——人们往往低估了职业生涯的漫长。其实我们有充足的时间去行动，让事情开花结果。这听起来可能有些高深，但我觉得马可·奥勒留说过，人生其实很长，只是我们把它用得很糟糕，浪费了太多时间。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I think you're so right, Lenny, and I love that because people are going around being like, "Life is short, life is short." But that's so true. We waste so much time. But also I think we don't recognize how much opportunity we have in front of us. And as a 26-year-old, I definitely thought my career was over. I was like, "I blew it." And looking back, it's funny.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同你的观点，莱尼。这点很棒，因为人们总爱感叹“人生短暂，人生短暂”。但这确实是真理。我们浪费了太多时间。但我觉得我们也意识不到面前有多少机遇。作为26岁的人，我曾坚信自己的职业生涯已经结束，心想“我把一切都搞砸了”。回首往事，这真是件趣事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I know exactly what you mean. I spent nine years at my first job at a random company in San Diego in a startup. I was like, "What am I doing here so long?" And it turned out that was really useful for the thing I did next. And then eventually, wow, things started to really take off. So I think that's a really good lesson for people. It's just a long time. This is my fourth career. I've switched careers many times. I was an engineer then. I was a founder. Then I was a product manager, and whatever this is. Whatever you call this thing.
turns.zh: 是啊，我完全理解你的意思。我在圣地亚哥一家初创公司工作了九年，感觉自己在这待太久了。结果这段经历为我后续的职业发展提供了宝贵经验。最终，哇，事情开始突飞猛进。所以我觉得这对人们来说是个很好的启示。时间很充裕。这是我第四次职业转型了。我换过很多次工作，先是工程师，再是创始人，然后是产品经理，现在又不知道该怎么称呼自己了。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: I guess me, too. I was an operator. I was a consultant. Well, I was an employee. I was a consultant. Then I was an operator, which is a fancy way to say employee at a startup. And then now I'm a founder and a VC and an angel and whatever this is..
turns.zh: 我也一样。我当过运营人员，咨询顾问，员工，后来又当了初创公司的运营主管。现在我成了创始人、风险投资人、天使投资人等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Awesome. So I think that's a really important takeaways. Just there's a lot of time to do stuff and don't stress if things aren't moving as fast as you want. I'm curious, what's a mess-up or a big mistake maybe that you made or your teammate that was like, "Oh wow, that was a big waste of time."
turns.zh: 太棒了。太棒了。所以我觉得这真是条重要启示。时间充裕，别因为事情进展不快就焦虑。我很好奇，你或者你的团队成员有没有犯过什么大错，或者后悔做过什么浪费时间的事。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Yeah, look, a lot of things didn't work out. More than 50% of our A/B tests didn't work out. We made bets that didn't make sense. I will say though, that in the spirit of A and B sides, I, and I think in general, we are really good at forgetting the B stuff. I talk so much about all the stuff that worked that it's hard to remember all of those moments that didn't actually work. And the thing that I tend to talk about, which is this mistake that we made as the growth team is almost like one of those, when you get asked in an interview, what's your biggest weakness, and you're like, "I'm a perfectionist." It's like one of those things that actually makes you sound good because it's the story about how my team really wanted to implement badges. We spent a lot of time playing all the games that were popular at the time, trying to understand how those gamification growth hacks that we could find in those apps would potentially overlay onto Duolingo and how we would do that. (00:53:35): And badges was just pervasive in all of the top games. And so it seemed like a no-brainer, but since we ranked all of our experiments in terms of ROI and return being like how many users we think we're going to get from this DAUs, and time investments, it never made sense to focus on this because we thought that the time sink would be too high. So I actually ended up not letting the team run this experiment for six months so that we focused on lower hanging fruit. So that's a mistake on my end. (00:54:04): Then we decided to run this experiment in the most lean way possible. We're like, "You know what? There's MVEs. There's minimum viable experiments. We don't have to run a whole badges thing. We can just do something more simple and actually see if that leads to growth in an interesting way, and then we'll know." (00:54:20): And we ran this very simple experiment that was like, you signed up and then you get a badge. And it was like this girl with a balloon. I don't know, she was happy or whatever. And of course in retrospect, it led to no results, because no one is proud of signing up. It's not an exciting moment, and you don't even have badges to collect. You can't show it to other people. None of the things that make badges compelling were there, but we were like, "Okay, well, we tested it didn't work." And then we moved on. (00:54:42): So we moved on for another, I don't know, eight months and we didn't look back. And then when we did look back, first of all at that point we discovered that we hadn't been dogfooding, which also was embarrassing. Looking back, we hadn't been dogfooding in the growth team. We just come up with hypotheses. We were super careful about prioritizing them and making sure that we were doing the best possible write ups and all these things. But the dogfooding piece, I didn't come from a product background. I was a marketer and I didn't really understand the term dogfooding, but when we thought, we had a conversation, we were like, "You know what? If we had just tested that, we would've all known that this was a super lame badge." And I was like, "Why are we not testing our experiments?" And so that became part of our practice. (00:55:26): It's still relevant. I just had a conversation yesterday with engineers at Latitud. I haven't explained what we built yet, where we're building it. Maybe we'll get there, but I was talking yesterday, [inaudible 00:55:35] at Latitud, and they're awesome. In terms of product team, we have the number eight employee at NewBank. You might've heard of NewBank, but it's this massive banking fintech in Latin America. And we have people from other fintechs. And then we have this guy who was a lead PM at Twilio, and I was explaining to them why we should be dogfooding. And they were all like, "Oh yeah, we should dogfood." It's just easy to forget stuff like that. (00:55:58): So that was a mistake that we could have probably gotten to the growth that we got to with badges much earlier on. And not only did we get to growth with badges, but it became this amazing treasure trove of opportunity because once you have badges and people want them, you can now ask people to do anything. Go find friends, go buy things, whatever it is. And so we impacted almost all metrics across the company positively, including some we hadn't expected, but it's easy to talk about a mistake that ended up being a win. So that's why I compared it to the interview thing in the beginning. But we tried making Duolingo a social app really early on and failed. It was called Dual Duels. Dual Duels. You could duel.
turns.zh:
是啊，你看，很多事情都不顺利。我们进行的A/B测试中有超过50%都不成功。我们做过一些不明智的决策。不过说实话，本着A和B两面的精神，我觉得我们真的很善于忘记那些失败的尝试。我总是在讲那些成功的案例，却很难记住那些最终没有效果的尝试。而我常提到的那个成长团队的错误，就像是在面试中被问到“你最大的弱点是什么”时回答“我是个完美主义者”一样。这听起来像是在自我吹嘘，但说实话，这其实暴露了我们团队当时想在Duolingo上推广徽章系统的野心。我们花了大量时间玩当时流行的游戏，试图理解那些应用中的游戏化增长黑客策略如何能应用到Duolingo上，但最后发现成本太高，不值得投入。于是我最终决定暂停这个实验六个月，让团队专注于更容易见效的项目。这确实是我的失误。

后来我们决定以最精简的方式进行实验。我们想：“没关系，既然有MVE（最小可行性实验），我们可以先做个简单测试，再看看是否能带来增长。”于是我们推出了一个简单到离谱的实验：注册后就能获得徽章，徽章图案是一个拿着气球的女孩。我不知道她为什么那么开心，但回想起来，结果很糟糕，因为用户对注册本身没什么自豪感，这根本不是什么激动人心的时刻，更别提收集徽章、向别人炫耀这些元素了。所有让徽章系统引人入胜的要素都缺失了，但我们还是坚持说：“好吧，我们测试了它，不成功。”然后就继续下一个项目了。

又过了八个月，我们才回头审视这个项目。首先发现，我们从未在成长团队内部进行过产品验证，这真是令人尴尬的。回想起来，我们甚至没有在成长团队内部进行过产品验证，只是提出假设、优先排序、撰写文档等，但完全忽略了产品验证环节。我当时没有产品背景，只是市场人员，根本不了解“dogfooding”这个术语。但当我们讨论时，我们意识到：“如果我们当时测试过那个徽章系统，我们早就发现它有多糟糕了。”我问：“为什么我们不测试实验结果呢？”于是我们开始重视产品验证环节。

这个问题至今仍有现实意义。昨天我和Latitud的工程师们交流时，还没来得及解释我们的产品方向。不过昨天在Latitud的对话让我很受启发。他们在产品团队方面堪称典范。我们是NewBank的第八号员工，可能你们听说过NewBank，这是一家大型金融科技公司。
比如在拉丁美洲市场，我们招募了来自其他金融科技公司的员工。还有一位曾在Twilio担任首席产品经理的同行，我向他们解释为何要开展内部测试（dogfooding）。他们都赞同说：“对呀，我们也应该这么做。”但有时人们很容易忽视这些关键细节。（00:55:58）这其实是个失误——其实我们本可以更早地借助徽章功能实现用户增长。不仅徽章功能推动了用户增长，更成为一个蕴藏巨大机遇的宝库。一旦徽章机制上线且用户对其产生需求，你就能赋予用户各种任务——比如邀请好友、购买商品等等。最终，我们几乎所有业务指标都实现了正向增长，其中有些成效甚至超出预期。回想起来，一个看似失误的决策最终却带来了丰厚回报，这正是创业过程中常有的“塞翁失马”效应。这也是我开篇将其与招聘面试相提并论的原因。不过，我们早期曾试图将Duolingo打造为社交应用，但最终以失败告终。那个项目叫“Dual Duels”（双人决斗），用户可以在其中进行对决游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very clever.
turns.zh: 真聪明。

turns.speaker: Gina Gotthilf
turns.en: Yeah, I know we were clever, but people didn't use it and we didn't figure out why. We tried making a Duolingo for schools platform. We couldn't get it to pick up. I went and watched dueling go in China and it got downloaded by a million people in the first day, and then the app got blocked because of the government, and then we couldn't figure out what to do. And then everyone rated the app like one star because it didn't work. And so then we had a lot of trouble actually recovering from that. We launched Duolingo in India and didn't realize because we couldn't have unless we went there, which we finally did, that most people set their phone UI in India to English, because typing in Hindi is hard. And of course there's a lot of languages throughout India, and we were making it so that when you downloaded Duolingo, whatever UI you open your app, your phone was set to, we offered not that language for you to learn. That was your base language. So we were telling people learn French, Spanish, German from English, and they were all trying to learn English, so they didn't find what they were looking for and they left. There were so many mistakes and luckily I think we were able to bounce back from most of them in terms of how Duolingo was doing today.
turns.zh: 是啊，我知道我们当时想法很巧妙，但用户没用这个功能，我们也不知道原因。我们曾试图开发一个面向学校的Duolingo平台，但没能成功推广。我去观察了中国版的《决斗之夜》，首日下载量就达百万，但因为政府封禁被下架了，然后我们又不知道该怎么办。用户给这个应用打了一星评价，因为根本用不了。从这件事中我们花了很长时间才恢复元气。后来我们在印度推出Duolingo，却没意识到除非亲自去当地，否则无法获取数据——印度用户普遍将手机UI设为英文，因为输入印地语太麻烦了。印度语言种类繁多，我们当时设计得是只要用户下载Duolingo，应用界面设定为当地语言，用户就能学习对应语言，结果大家都想学英语，导致他们找不到想要的内容然后离开了。我们犯了太多错误，所幸大部分问题都能通过如今Duolingo的成功得以弥补。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And our final story is from Maggie Crowley VP of product at Toast, and one of the most beloved episodes of the podcast. This is Maggie sharing something a little bit different, her favorite interview question about failure and what it tells you about the person you're interviewing. Plus a story of her own product failure. Here's Maggie.
turns.zh: 最后一位嘉宾是Toast公司的产品副总裁Maggie Crowley，这也是播客中最受欢迎的一期节目。Maggie分享了她对失败的看法，以及她自己产品失败的经历。下面是Maggie的发言。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: A question I ask in every product interview is, what's the worst product you've ever shipped? And that's because I don't think you're a good PM if you haven't shipped something that's really shitty. You just haven't had enough reps, you haven't done it enough times. And it's not only that you've done it, but that you can admit it and which one it is. That's so important. (00:58:34): I remember... It was so dumb. I'm still so mad about this that we did this. I won't name which team, which company, I'm not going to call that out, but we decided we needed to do a rewrite red flag number one of existing product, and engineer who I'd worked with many times, we had a really good relationship and this person was like, "Yeah, yeah, it's going to take six months. No problem." Core part of the product, been around for forever. One of those things that the code is still the code written by the founders kind of thing. (00:59:07): It didn't take six months. It took two and a half years. It still wasn't done. It almost never... It went on for so much longer than it should have. It took us forever to get to feature parody. It was the worst project. So many people rotated in and out of it. Everyone thought it was dumb. Sunk cost fallacy, just the worst. And it's because, A, we got arrogant and we thought we could do it. B, we skipped discovery. We didn't really write a one pager. We just went for it. We didn't do enough technical and design research into what the requirements would actually have to be. And there you have it.
turns.zh: 我在每次产品面试中都会问一个问题：你发布过的最失败的产品是什么？因为我认为，如果一个产品经理没有推出过真正烂透了的产品，那他就不够优秀。这不仅说明你有过足够的尝试次数，更重要的是你能承认失败并说出失败之处。这太重要了。（00:58:34）：我记得……那真是太蠢了。我们做这个项目至今还很生气。虽然我不会点名哪个团队、哪家公司，但我们决定重写现有产品的核心功能。当时和我合作过多次的工程师，我们关系很好，他说：“没问题，就六个月。”但核心部分已经存在多年了，代码还是创始人写的原始版本。（00:59:07）：结果没用六个月，用了两年半。还是没完成。几乎从未……耗时远超预期。我们花了很久才实现功能平移。这是最失败的项目。太多人来来去去，每个人都觉得这项目很蠢。陷入沉没成本谬论，简直糟透了。主要原因是，A，我们太自大，觉得自己能行。B，我们跳过了探索阶段。我们甚至没写一份产品概要，直接就上马了。我们没有充分调研技术和设计需求。就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And did not work out, or was it a huge success in the end and it changed the trajectory of the business?
turns.zh: 那这个项目最后是失败了，还是最终大获成功，改变了公司的发展轨迹？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Absolutely not. But you know what? I didn't get fired, so it's fine.
turns.zh: 绝对不行。但你知道吗？我没被解雇，所以还好啦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I've gone through those experiences and then three, four years later, it's like another... Maybe this rewrite and redesign may work. We haven't updated this thing in a long time.
turns.zh: 我感觉自己经历过那些事，然后三四年后，又来一次……也许这次重写和重新设计能行得通。我们好久没更新这个东西了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Just don't do it. Don't rewrite. If anyone ever tells you to do a rewrite, don't do it. A side-by-side rewrite, nope.
turns.zh: 千万别这么做。别重写。要是有人让你重写，千万别答应。那种边写边改的重写，千万别干。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've never had... What I run into is once you get too far down a redesign slash rewrite, everyone's building in that new world, and then you launch, and experiment's negative, and then it's just like, "Oh, we just got to launch it. We're going to call it back. We're going to figure out how to get back to neutral someday."
turns.zh: 是啊，我从没遇到过……我遇到的情况是，一旦你深入到重新设计或重写的阶段，每个人都在那个新世界里埋头工作，然后上线后，实验结果不理想，就只能说：“哦，赶紧上线吧，总会有办法回到正轨的。”

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah yeah. Don't do that.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。别这么做。
